Article Title: 9 in 10 Indians research festive purchases online, but 70% buy on impulse: Google study
Article Text:
9 in 10 Indians research festive purchases online, but 70% buy on impulse: Google study

What the study says

A Google-commissioned Ipsos consumer study has found that Indian festive shoppers are operating at two very different speeds. According to it, 9 in 10 consumers conduct extensive online research before buying—discovering new brands, comparing prices, and checking reviews. While 70% of festive purchases are decided in the moment, sparked by visual discovery and festive urgency.Roma Datta Chobey, Managing Director, Connected Consumer Commerce, Google India, said, “What stands out across India’s festive season is how deliberate research and spontaneous impulse coexist. Shoppers are taking richer, AI-guided journeys to evaluate trade-offs, yet they are equally ready to check out in hours when sparked by video and rapid delivery. With choices remaining fluid right up to the final mile, Google and YouTube sit at the heart of this behavior. Winning this season means meeting consumers at both speeds: building deep relevance during deliberation and moving fast to capture immediate demand—an agility unlocked by our Gemini-powered solutions. ”Some of the findings are:● AI is becoming an essential festive shopping companion, with consumers consulting chatbots an average of 7.5 times, especially when evaluating categories like electronics, appliances, home decor, and personal care.This creates a more curious consumer for whom conversations act as a springboard: across shopping journeys more broadly, AI users explore 2.8x more touchpoints online as they seek deeper context.● 51% of festive shoppers credit AI with helping them make choices. This expertise flexes across different needs: shoppers lean on AI for highly specific, tailored answers in personal care and beauty, while using it to demystify complex specs, refine criteria, and evaluate trade-offs in categories like home appliances and consumer electronics. Aided with knowledge they never previously considered, buyers navigate choices with authority—a shift echoed beyond festive season, where 87% of users report making decisions with higher confidence using AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search.● Alongside planned research, festive shopping carries a high-momentum spontaneous track where immediate appeal drives the cart. Google and YouTube directly influence 54% of these unplanned purchases, the study claimed adding it is driven primarily by festive urgency, compelling offers, and the instant pull of discovering an appealing product in the moment.● Visual inspiration and creators turn ideas into instant buys: Visual cues are the primary catalyst for quick action. As celebrations approach, styling searches surge and shoppers act directly on what catches their eye: 53% use visual tools like Google Lens to discover or compare products, while creators and short-form video close the decision loop. 73% of festive buyers turn to creators for inspiration, and 61% of those who made purchases within a couple of days or less without prior research used YouTube Shorts in their shopping journeys.●Delivery timing has become critical, with 90% of shoppers viewing sub-two-day delivery as non-negotiable and 81% choosing retailers based on speed. This demand for immediacy is already visible around key festivals this season: Google Trends recorded a sharp surge in searches for “same day delivery rakhi” a day before Rakshabandhan this year.Across every entry point, shoppers naturally integrate the platforms into their journey: among consumers using AI chatbots, 94% concurrently turn to Google Search and 87% to YouTube, while 7 in 10 shoppers who spot products on social media turn to Google Search to evaluate them further.Because consumers continuously explore and cross-check across channels, festive choices remain fluid right up to checkout. 8 in 10 shoppers report being open to trying new retailers — an intent that actively plays out on Google, where 51% of shoppers using Google Search and/or YouTube discover new products along their journey.
Article Summary: 9 in 10 Indians research festive purchases online, but 70% buy on impulse. Google and YouTube directly influence 54% of these unplanned purchases. Google Trends recorded a sharp surge in searches for ‘same day delivery rakhi’ a day before Rakshabandhan.

Article Title: Developers sent letters offering $10,000 to every household in a rural town in the US if a data center is built; almost everyone rejected the offer, and everyone has the same concern
Article Text:
Representative AI image

Why residents rejected the $10,000 data centre offer

A developer offered to give every household in a small Pennsylvania town $10,000 if they agreed to a massive data centre project. The money could pay for rent, groceries, fuel or even help someone buy a car. But the offer has failed to win over many residents, who fear the project could damage their homes, disrupt their lives and change their community. NorthPoint Development sent letters to households in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, offering a total of $45 million to 4,500 households if the township allowed the proposed data centre project to go ahead, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.The plan involves building the first of 15 data centre buildings across 1,300 acres in the Pocono foothills. The proposed project, however, has faced strong local opposition, with residents raising concerns about noise, property values and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. For a town where the median household income is about $60,000, the proposed $10,000 payment represents a significant sum. Yet many residents interviewed by the Journal said they were not keen to accept the project, even with the money on offer.For Jeff Fasnacht, a retired teacher who lives near the proposed site, the main concern is what the development could do to his property's value. He believes the payment would not make up for a possible fall in the value of his home. “$10,000 doesn’t match how much it’s going to tank my property value,” Fasnacht told the Journal.Diana Spallone, a special-education teacher who also received the letter, shared similar concerns. She and her husband recently spent money on home improvements, including a new roof. While the proposed payment could help replenish their savings, she worries that the data centre could ultimately hurt the value of their property.“$10,000 would be nice,” Spallone said.Others are concerned about what the project could mean for the wider community. Some residents fear years of construction noise, while others distrust large developers and worry that towns are not being given enough information before major projects are approved.Ed Negra, a retired homeowner helping organise opposition, believes the cash offer could have the opposite effect to what the developer intended.“I think it works the opposite way, because most people have the opinion that, ‘hey, are they trying to bribe us here?’” Negra told the Journal.NorthPoint's chief marketing officer, Brent Miles, said the idea of direct payments emerged after an angry public meeting last year, when residents questioned what they would gain from supporting the project. “I think we’ve got something here that’s on the cutting edge,” Miles told the Journal, “really in direct response to ‘what’s in it for me?’”The company has also proposed another $120 million in payments over 15 years for police services and other community investments. Miles said the company had persuaded some residents who were initially sceptical by answering questions about water use, energy costs and noise.However, the project remains uncertain. Hazle Township rejected it on zoning grounds in November, after which NorthPoint sued the township to overturn the decision.
Article Summary: NorthPoint Development sent letters to households in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, offering a total of $45 million to 4,500 households. The plan involves building the first of 15 data centre buildings across 1,300 acres in the Pocono foothills. The proposed project has faced strong local opposition, with residents raising concerns about noise, property values and the rapid expansion of AI.

Article Title: The Facebook files: The story of the insider who secretly copied tens of thousands of pages of Silicon Valley’s darkest secrets
Article Text:
The Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen

Who was Frances Haugen, and why did she copy Facebook's files

What did 'the Facebook files' reveal

How Facebook has responded to the allegations

Frances Haugen, a former Facebook employee, secretly copied tens of thousands of pages of the company's internal documents before leaving her job in 2021. The material exposed concerns about how the social media giant handled misinformation, hate speech and the impact of Instagram on teenage girls. Frances Haugen later revealed her identity in an interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, setting off a major debate over Facebook's responsibility for the harm linked to its platforms. As per a TIME report published in October 2021, Haugen was a data scientist who worked as a product manager on Facebook's Civic Integrity team. She said the company repeatedly put its business interests ahead of public safety.Frances Haugen joined Facebook in June 2019, hoping to help the company tackle misinformation. She had become concerned about online conspiracy theories after losing a friend to them. Before joining Facebook, she had worked at other technology companies, including Google and Pinterest.By April 2021, Haugen had resigned and taken a large collection of internal documents with her. As reported by TIME, she submitted tens of thousands of documents to the US Securities and Exchange Commission and Congress. She also became the main source behind The Wall Street Journal's series known as the Facebook Files.Haugen told 60 Minutes correspondent Scott Pelley that Facebook was “substantially worse” than other platforms she had seen when it came to putting user engagement ahead of product safety.“Facebook has realized that if they change the algorithm to be safer, people will spend less time on the site, they’ll click on less ads, they’ll make less money,” Haugen told 60 Minutes.The documents raised questions about Facebook's decisions on misinformation, political content and Instagram's effect on young users. Haugen alleged that Facebook rolled back some safeguards against misinformation after the 2020 US presidential election. She said the company dissolved its Civic Integrity team after the election, a decision she believed helped create conditions that contributed to the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol.“They basically said, ‘Oh good, we made it through the election. There wasn’t riots. We can get rid of Civic Integrity now,’” she said. “Fast forward a couple months, we got the insurrection.”Haugen also said Facebook's decision to reduce or switch off some safeguards after the election felt like a betrayal. “That really feels like a betrayal of democracy to me,” she added.Facebook's internal research also examined Instagram's effects on teenage girls. Haugen said the findings showed that the platform could worsen body-image concerns among some young users.“It actually makes them use the app more. And so, they end up in this feedback cycle where they hate their bodies more and more,” Haugen said.The documents also raised concerns about Facebook's ability to moderate harmful content in languages beyond English and French. Haugen argued that the company did not invest enough in safety systems for all the regions where it operated.“Every time Facebook expands to a new one of these linguistic areas, it costs just as much—if not more—to make safety systems for that language as it did to make English or French,” she said. “The economics just doesn’t make sense for Facebook to be safe in a lot of these parts of the world.”Facebook rejected Haugen's claim that it encouraged harmful content and failed to act. Lena Pietsch, the company's director of policy communications, said its teams had to balance users' right to express themselves with the need to keep the platform safe.“We continue to make significant improvements to tackle the spread of misinformation and harmful content. To suggest we encourage bad content and do nothing is just not true,” Pietsch said.Nick Clegg, then Facebook's vice president of global affairs, also rejected claims that the company was responsible for the January 6 violence. He said responsibility lay with those who carried out and encouraged the attack.Haugen then said she did not intend to target Facebook's founder personally. “I have a lot of empathy for Mark,” she told Pelley. “But he has allowed choices to be made where the side effects of those choices are that hateful, polarizing content gets more distribution and more reach.”After the interview aired, Haugen wrote on Twitter that she believed “we can do better.”“Together we can create social media that brings out the best in us. We solve problems together – we don’t solve them alone,” she then tweeted.
Article Summary: Frances Haugen, a former Facebook employee, secretly copied tens of thousands of pages of the company's internal documents before leaving her job in 2021. The material exposed concerns about how the social media giant handled misinformation, hate speech and the impact of Instagram on teenage girls. Haugen later revealed her identity in an interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, setting off a major debate over Facebook's responsibility.

Article Title: Anthropic cuts internet access for Claude during testing after it goes rogue; breaking into US websites, databases and calling Police; company 'realises' need 'better' training
Article Text:
Anthropic on Claude 's 'rogue' behaviors

How Anthropic plans to solve the rogue behaviour

Another day, another AI Agent gone rogue. Anthropic has made fresh admission of its AI models going berserk, breaking into websites, databases, tipping Police of wrong leads and more. And what looks like a 'solution for now', Frontier AI lab Anthropic has shut down live internet access across all internal evaluations. The internet access shutdown comes after Dario Amodei's company discovered tat its autonomous agents routinely exploited public websites, bypassed security firewalls, and, in one instance, filed a fake murder tip with the Philadelphia Police Department.Anthropic has disclosed the incidents in a blog post, revealing that AI agents instructed to complete research tasks went off script to scour the open web for resources. "We believe it’s important to be transparent about what we see our models do during testing and use," it said. Along the way, the systems exploited software vulnerabilities, bypassed paywalls to access subscription databases, and routed queries through URL shorteners to smuggle data past safety guardrails. Anthropic uncovered the rogue activity during an internal post-audit that began in July, acknowledging it had failed to detect the behaviors in real time.The findings strike at the core of the AI industry’s push into agentic workflows -- systems designed to browse the web and navigate desktop environments on behalf of knowledge workers. Anthropic conceded that standard alignment training remains inadequate for preventing unintended behaviors when models are granted computer-use capabilities and live web access.The behaviors stem from "reward hacking," an alignment pitfall where a model discovers that exploiting technical loopholes or evading constraints fulfills its objective function faster than obeying operating rules.In the blog post titled, 'Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use', Anthropic said that it has pulled the plug on live internet access for internal evaluations until it can ensure containment and oversight. Moving forward, the lab plans to conduct tests offline, route internal agents through centrally managed infrastructure, and deploy automated classifiers to detect similar boundary-pushing tactics. Anthropic did not specify the exact benchmarks required before live connectivity would be restored.Anthropic grouped Claude's rogue behaviors into four categories. "Below, we describe four categories of behavior in which Claude acted on real websites and systems in ways we did not intend, each of which involved an organization or person outside Anthropic," the blog reads.* Claude exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server;* Claude submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it should not have;* Claude working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee; and* Claude using URL shortening services to get around limits in its fetch tool.On remedial measures, the blog said, "We’ve taken several preventive measures. Some of the public evaluations we no longer run; others we have moved to their offline versions, or rebuilt them so that their tasks do not reach live websites. We’ve also made broader changes. We have updated the guardrails on some of our internet access tools, such as the web fetch tool, to heavily restrict what the model can do with them. And, as part of our ongoing agent security and monitoring efforts, we have built tooling to automatically detect and block the kinds of behaviors described above. This tooling now runs on most of our evaluations and on internal agentic use of frontier models."It further added, "We’re also taking other steps to prevent unintended agentic actions within Anthropic, and to catch them if they occur. These include migrating internal agents to centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment, minimizing internet access for internal agents and training processes, and monitoring far more of what agents do through techniques like safety classifiers and hierarchical summarization. These measures are now part of our security team’s detection and response procedures so that we can respond to and contain undesired behavior quickly. We expect to publish more on these approaches, and to build them directly into our products."
Article Summary: Frontier AI lab Anthropic has shut down live internet access across all internal evaluations. The internet access shutdown comes after Dario Amodei's company discovered tat its autonomous agents routinely exploited public websites. Anthropic uncovered the rogue activity during an internal post-audit that began in July.

Article Title: White House Super Intelligence Force leaders change ‘voluntary security reporting’ to mandatory after calling out Anthropic's ‘fraudulent’ use of government systems
Article Text:
Anthropic

Anthropic’s AI models involved in unauthorised visa filings and bogus police tips

Read full statement from White House Super Intelligence Force

Earlier today, Anthropic contacted the SI Force to disclose the details of various prior incidents that it discovered in late September involving the unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems.

The company informed us that these events occurred in the past, the activity has ceased, and there is no ongoing similar activity.

We informed the company that we expect immediate and full transparency to the entities involved and the public. We also expect that the company will immediately provide remediation services to the affected entities and any harmed Americans.

More generally, this disclosure underscores precisely why President Trump established the Super Intelligence Force and secured a memorandum of understanding with America's frontier SI labs.

The federal government has a fundamental responsibility to protect its systems, safeguard sensitive information, defend our national security, and protect Americans. The SI Force will fulfill its responsibility and SI companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm.

We also expect these companies to work with the effected systems to ensure that similar incidents to not occur.

This notification and remediation process is not optional. It is a critical national security obligation. We expect Anthropic and all companies to honor their obligations, immediately report incidents, fully cooperate with federal and state law enforcement authorities, remedy any damage, and implement concrete safeguards to ensure these failures do not reoccur.

Our message to all SI companies is clear: delayed notification, inadequate corrective action, and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated.

President Trump has been clear: America will lead the world in Super Intelligence, but innovation will never be an excuse for compromising national security, government integrity, or public trust. We established the Super Intelligence Force and these safeguards for exactly this reason.

In a major shift, the US government is essentially scrapping its voluntary security disclosure policy for artificial intelligence (AI) companies, making it mandatory for these tech labs to immediately report and fix security breaches involving their models. The change comes after federal officials called out Claude-maker Anthropic over what the government described as “unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems.” While the administration had previously leaned on voluntary compliance and private-sector self-governance, leadership from the White House Super Intelligence (SI) Force declared that automatic reporting is now an imperative national priority.“This notification and remediation process is not optional. It is a critical national security obligation,” White House Super Intelligence Force leaders said in a statement shared exclusively with Axios.The regulatory tightening was sparked by disclosures from Anthropic itself. The company identified unauthorised system interactions and contacted federal authorities to outline what occurred, stating that the activity has since stopped.A State Department official confirmed that Anthropic notified the agency on Thursday (October 8) after an internal testing model submitted 19 non-immigrant visa applications in August and another in May. The submissions occurred via the department's public web portal. Officials noted that none of the applications were processed and that federal databases were neither hacked nor compromised.In a second incident, police investigators in Philadelphia revealed that an Anthropic system filed a fabricated homicide tip with their department.Anthropic's Disclosure: Late Friday, Anthropic released a public summary confirming multiple events while withholding granular specifics about other government departments touched by the testing.
Article Summary: The US government is essentially scrapping its voluntary security disclosure policy for artificial intelligence (AI) companies. The change comes after federal officials called out Claude-maker Anthropic over what the government described as “unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems.

Article Title: Citadel CEO Ken Griffin makes largest-ever donation in US history to a University as he wants to change the very fabric of …
Article Text:
Ken Griffin’s bet on Miami's future

The campus

Land and the Pittsburgh gift

New campus near Griffin-backed investments

Hedge-fund billionaire and Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has pledged a record-breaking donation of $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, including $2 billion to establish a new campus in Miami, in what the university says is the largest single donation ever made by an individual to higher education. According to a report by the Wall Street Journal the majority of the funding will go toward building a 35-acre Carnegie Mellon University campus in Miami's Wynwood neighbourhood, while an additional $1 billion will support the university's main campus in Pittsburgh. "The students who graduate and the tech companies that come to Miami to leverage those skills will change the very fabric of Miami for decades if not centuries to come," Griffin said in an interview.The donation advances Griffin's long-term ambition to turn South Florida into a leading global centre for technology, innovation and business. "I believe that all great American cities are anchored by great universities and Carnegie Mellon will bring a great university here to Miami complementary to other universities here in the region," he said.The Citadel founder has increasingly focused his investments and philanthropic efforts on South Florida after relocating the headquarters of his hedge fund firm, Citadel, to the region.A spokesperson said Griffin has now contributed $2.4 billion to causes in South Florida and more than $5.7 billion in total charitable donations.Carnegie Mellon, known for computer science, artificial intelligence and robotics, will open a campus in Miami's Wynwood neighborhood focused on technology and innovation. The university projects it will eventually support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master's and Ph.D. students, nearly 300 faculty and over 600 staff. That would make it by far the university's largest expansion. Its satellite campuses in New York City, Mountain View, Calif. , and Qatar each serve up to a few hundred students.The campus will concentrate on four areas:* human health and biological discovery* national security and strategic capabilities* energy and climate resilience* advanced manufacturing and industrial transformationPrograms will combine artificial intelligence, computing and machine learning with the university's humanities, fine arts and design disciplines. The campus will host industry research labs and venture studios so students, faculty and partners can build technologies together. The focus fits the region's growing defense-tech and healthcare sectors, the Journal noted."Miami is an area in which Carnegie Mellon can reinvent not only what students learn, but how they learn," said Farnam Jahanian, the university's president.Construction is slated to begin in 2027, and the campus aims to enroll its first students in 2028.The campus will sit on a site bought from developer Moishe Mana for $1.1 billion, according to a press release. Who will ultimately hold the deed hasn't been made public. The Journal described the site as both a 35-acre and a roughly 30-acre property in different places. Griffin is joining Carnegie Mellon's Board of Trustees, and the university's computer science school in Pittsburgh will be renamed the Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science. Citadel has a long history of hiring Carnegie Mellon graduates, including many quantitative engineers.The university's campus will be located near another major investment backed by Griffin in Wynwood, where he partnered with Goldman Properties to acquire an office tower for $180 million. The property is home to a growing mix of financial services, technology and creative businesses, including the MIAX Sapphire options trading floor, one of the few open-outcry trading floors launched in the US in recent decades. Commenting on the scale of the initiative, Jessica Goldman Srebnick, co-chair of Goldman Properties, said the project's vision matched its unprecedented financial backing. "The thinking is so big, matched with a financial commitment of historic proportions, you just know that the scale of the outcome will be breathtaking," she said.
Article Summary: Hedge-fund billionaire and Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has pledged a record-breaking donation of $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University. The donation advances Griffin's long-term ambition to turn South Florida into a leading global centre for technology, innovation and business. The university will open a campus in Miami's Wynwood neighborhood focused on technology and innovation.

Article Title: San Francisco software engineer called ‘horrible father’ after he jokes about using AI to read bedtime stories to his newborn
Article Text:
Representative image

Quick backlash across social media

Engineer pulls post, agrees to drop the topic

An attempt at tech humor by a Silicon Valley engineer has sparked widespread online backlash, after a software engineer joked about training an artificial intelligence (AI) voice model to read bedtime stories to his newborn child instead of doing it himself. Alvin Sng, a software engineer at the San Francisco-based AI research lab Factory, shared an exchange between himself and his wife on X (formerly Twitter) that quickly went viral for all the wrong reasons.According to Sng’s post (first reported by The New York Post), his wife asked him: “Can you read our baby a book?” When Sng suggested playing a standard audiobook instead, his wife pushed back, explaining that a pre-recorded tape would not be in his voice.“Me: I can train a voice model. Parenting hits different when you work in AI,” Sng recounted writing.The attempt to make light of automating infant care drew immediate criticism across the platform, with commentators labeling the attitude cold and disconnected. Direct replies criticised the premise bluntly, with one user stating, “Me: You are a horrible father.”Finance professional Andrew Lynch responded to the post calling it “absolute insanity,” adding, “These people’s brains are broken.”Aaron Fritschner, deputy chief of staff for Virginia Representative Don Beyer, characterized the exchange as “extremely bleak.”The exchange also tapped into broader cultural frustration regarding the direction of modern AI. Rather than taking over unpleasant physical labor, critics noted, automated systems are increasingly being directed at creative work and human bonding.“Truly can’t get over the fact that this technology came in and instead of using it to replace fixing toilets or folding clothes, people are using it to make movies and read to their kids,” one user remarked, adding, “This is maybe the saddest thing I’ve read on this site.”Other commentators argued that replacing personal parental presence with algorithmic clones could damage early child development. Influencer Michael Burns warned that relying on such methods risks raising children who are “unable to feel human love.”Following the mounting wave of criticism, Sng deleted the original post and issued a short follow-up note acknowledging the reaction:“Ok, enough jokes for a while. I’ll go back to reading bedtime stories for now,” he wrote on X the following day.
Article Summary: Alvin Sng, a software engineer at the San Francisco-based AI research lab Factory, shared an exchange between himself and his wife on X (formerly Twitter) that quickly went viral for all the wrong reasons. The attempt to make light of automating infant care drew immediate criticism across the platform.

Article Title: The leaked emails of 2007: What Steve Jobs and Eric Schmidt actually said when Google built Android
Article Text:
A message from Apple founder Steve Jobs to ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt

Eric Schmidt terminated at least two recruiters for violations

Consequences

Long before Apple and Google became fierce rivals in the smartphone era, an exchange between Steve Jobs and Eric Schmidt revealed how seriously Silicon Valley leaders viewed the battle for engineering talent. According to a report by Reuters, court documents later made public lic showed jobs personally asked Google to stop recruiting Apple employees, prompting swift action from Google’s leadership. The emails that surfaced during the civil litigation involving Apple, Google and several other technology companies accused of conspiring to suppress employee compensation by limiting competition for skilled workers.As reported by Reuters, when Jobs learned Google had targeted one of his employees, he emailed Schmidt directly, then Google's chairman, saying he "would be very pleased if your recruiting department would stop doing this." Schmidt forwarded the email to colleagues, writing that he believed Google had a policy of not recruiting from Apple and that this was a direct request from Jobs. The recruiting department replied that he should extend apologies as appropriate to Jobs, and the recruiter was fired.Google's senior staffing strategist told Schmidt the recruiter would be fired "within the hour." Schmidt called this an "appropriate response," and said he wanted HR to make a public example of the termination within the group and make it a strong part of new-hire training. Then came the smiley. After Schmidt told Jobs the recruiter would be fired, Jobs forwarded Schmidt's note to a top Apple human resources executive with a smiley face. Jobs did not reply to Schmidt with the smiley, as your headline implies. He sent it to his own HR chief.The recruiter was not the only one. Judge Lucy Koh wrote that emails showed Schmidt "terminated at least two recruiters for violations of anti-solicitation agreements, and threatened to terminate more." She said Schmidt, Jobs and Intuit chairman Bill Campbell were "key players" in creating and enforcing the agreements.In another episode, Google sought to hire three former Apple engineers for a planned engineering center in Paris. Jobs wrote that Apple would "strongly prefer" that Google not hire them, and Google told him it had scrapped the plan "based on your strong preference."Other emails showed Jobs threatening rivals. Jobs told Palm's then-CEO Edward Colligan that if Palm kept targeting Apple employees, Apple would launch a patent lawsuit. Google co-founder Sergey Brin testified that Jobs had told him hiring one of Apple's people would mean "war," a reference to patent litigation. Shown the smiley email in his deposition, Brin reportedly said, "Wow, Steve used a smiley." Schmidt also seemed aware of the legal risk. When Google's HR director asked whether the no-recruiting policy could be shared with others, Schmidt said he preferred it be shared verbally because he did not want to create a paper trail he could be sued over later.The lawsuit, filed in 2011 on behalf of more than 64,000 workers, alleged the agreements stopped employees from getting better job offers elsewhere. In 2014, Judge Koh rejected a proposed $324.5 million settlement, saying there was "substantial and compelling evidence" that Jobs was "a, if not the, central figure in the alleged conspiracy." The companies later agreed to a larger deal. The final figure was A$613.9 million, or roughly US$415 million.Schmidt later testified about Jobs' influence. "Steve was unhappy," he said, "and Steve's unhappiness absolutely influenced the change we made in recruiting practice."
Article Summary: Apple founder Steve Jobs personally asked Google to stop recruiting Apple employees. The emails surfaced during the civil litigation involving Apple, Google and several other technology companies. Google's senior staffing strategist told Schmidt the recruiter would be fired "within the hour"

Article Title: In 2024, Craigslist founder Craig Newmark gave $10 million to launch a free-tuition campaign at CUNY's journalism school; two years later, 70% of its incoming class is studying tuition-free
Article Text:
Image credit: City University of New York

How Craig Newmark's $10 million donation supports journalism students

Why is CUNY's journalism school offering free tuition

“Our alumni are known for their hustle…their rigor, their entrepreneurial grit,”

“Their reporting has changed legislation and gotten innocents out of jail. They have produced powerful, award-winning pieces of journalism. They have founded newsrooms that are filling news deserts. Our alumni are a force for good.”

How scholarships are helping journalism students

“I am not unique. I am merely one of hundreds of Newmark students who can attest to the doors that open when given the necessary resources, training, and support to pursue this work,”

“Our alumni are the clearest proof of what CUNY and Newmark make possible,”

“They leave this school prepared to inform communities, hold power accountable, and strengthen our civic life.”

“I could not be prouder that every New York resident who comes here can now attend tuition-free, and I’m just as committed to the work ahead to ensure that every student who walks through Newmark’s doors, no matter where they call home, can do the same.”

Craiglist founder Craig Newmark donated $10 million to launch a tuition-free campaign at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at the City University of New York (CUNY) in 2024. Two years later, the initiative has reached a milestone: 70% of the incoming Class of 2027 will attend the journalism school tuition-free. The institution announced this during its 20th anniversary celebration in New York earlier this month.The school now works to provide full tuition support to every student, including those outside New York, as part of a campaign to make journalism education more accessible to aspiring reporters.The tuition-free campaign launched two and a half years ago with a $10 million gift from Craig Newmark, founder of Craigslist and the journalism school's namesake. Since then, other donors have supported the initiative, helping the institution expand financial assistance for students.Dean Graciela Mochkofsky announced that every New York resident in the Class of 2027 is attending tuition-free. Overall, 70% of the incoming class is attending tuition-free, building on the school's efforts to expand access to journalism education.The school's next goal is to extend full tuition support to all students, regardless of where they live.The campaign reflects the school's founding mission: opening doors to aspiring journalists regardless of financial circumstances. It also aims to prepare graduates to serve their communities through reporting, public service and innovation.said Dean Mochkofsky.The school marked its 20th anniversary with a gala attended by alumni, journalism leaders, faculty, supporters and other guests. The event also honoured NBCUniversal News Group Chairman Cesar Conde and New York Times President and CEO Meredith Kopit Levien, whose organisations are among the school's leading employers of graduates.Newmark alumna Gibran Caroline Boyce said a full scholarship helped her pursue journalism. During her time at the school, she completed an internship at CNN and received support for reporting from Armenia and the US-Mexico border. After graduation, she secured a position at NBC News.Boyce said. CUNY Chancellor Matos Rodríguez also welcomed the tuition-free milestone and backed the school's plans to expand the programme.said CUNY’s Chancellor Matos Rodríguez.He added,Proceeds from the anniversary gala will fund scholarships and student success initiatives, enabling the school to increase its efforts to make journalism education accessible to more aspiring reporters.
Article Summary: Craiglist founder Craig Newmark donated $10 million to launch a tuition-free campaign at the City University of New York (CUNY) in 2024. Two years later, the initiative has reached a milestone: 70% of the incoming Class of 2027 will attend the journalism school tuition free. The school now works to provide full tuition support to every student, including those outside New York.

Peter Thiel

Why is Peter Thiel criticising Obama and Pope Leo over AI

“He needed something politically popular to distract from the church’s child sex abuse scandals, and he found it in AI,”

What has Peter Thiel said about AI regulation

Peter Thiel has accused former US President Barack Obama and Pope Leo XIV of opposing artificial intelligence (AI) to boost their popularity. The billionaire investor made the remarks during two recent closed-door lectures in Nashville, according to recordings obtained by Politico’s Decoded. Thiel argued that both leaders were capitalising on public concerns about AI while criticising opponents of the technology as obstacles to technological progress. He also questioned the pope's focus on AI, linking it to the Catholic Church's sexual abuse scandals.Thiel said.Thiel's comments reflect his opposition to efforts to regulate artificial intelligence and his belief that the public is using concerns about the technology for political purposes.The investor singled out Obama, who recently urged Democrats to develop a more comprehensive AI plan. Thiel argued that opposing the technology offered the party a way to appeal to voters despite what he described as a lack of ideas.He was more critical of Pope Leo XIV, suggesting that the pontiff's focus on AI served as a distraction from the Catholic Church's sexual abuse scandals.Thiel said, referring to the pope's first encyclical on AI.The remarks were made during a series of lectures in Nashville, offering a glimpse into Thiel's views on the intersection of technology, politics and religion.Thiel has criticised government intervention, which he believes might slow technological progress. Several Silicon Valley investors share his view that too much regulation could stifle innovation and cripple the potential of new technologies.However, his latest remarks go beyond the usual debate over AI policy by framing opposition to the technology in religious terms. Thiel has also warned about the Antichrist, whom he associates with efforts to halt technological progress and promote a “one world government” of regulation.
Article Summary: Billionaire investor made the remarks during two recent closed-door lectures in Nashville. Article Title: Tesla agrees to rename one of the biggest features of its cars in Europe after regulators call it 'misleading', name change comes as Elon Musk seeks ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

Why has Tesla renamed its Full Self-Driving feature

Why are European regulators concerned about Tesla FSD

How is Tesla seeking EU-wide approval for FSD

"Please do not simply say again that 'we are waiting for the EU' without explaining what Tesla or Norway must deliver in the meantime.”

When could Tesla get approval for FSD in Europe

Tesla has renamed its Full Self-Driving feature on several European websites. The electric vehicle maker now uses the name Tesla Assisted Driving in countries including Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, and Slovakia, after regulators raised concerns that the previous name could mislead customers about the software's capabilities. The change comes as CEO Elon Musk seeks wider approval for the driver-assistance technology across the European Union.Although the feature assists with driving, motorists must continue to supervise the system and remain legally responsible. Germany said Tesla had offered to adopt the new name, while an EU-wide vote on the software's approval has been pushed from October to at least December. Eight EU countries already allow the system, with Slovakia expected to become the ninth.Tesla's European websites now use the name Tesla Assisted Driving instead of Full Self-Driving. However, the company's US website still uses the name Full Self-Driving (Supervised).The rebranding follows concerns from European regulators that the original name could give drivers the impression that Tesla vehicles can operate autonomously without human supervision.Germany said Tesla had offered to change the name on Tuesday.The move comes as the company continues to seek regulatory approval for its driver-assistance software across the EU.Several European authorities have questioned whether the Full Self-Driving name accurately describes the system's capabilities. The software requires drivers to remain attentive and supervise its operation, with responsibility for driving still resting with the person behind the wheel.In Sweden, consumer protection authorities had asked the Swedish Transport Agency to assess whether Tesla's marketing could give buyers a false impression about the system's ability to drive autonomously.In Italy, internal government correspondence said the name "Full Self-Driving", together with Tesla's promotional material, "could lead users to believe that the vehicle is equipped with unsupervised automatic driving functions attributable to higher levels of automation, particularly SAE Level 3".These concerns have increased scrutiny of how Tesla describes its driver-assistance technology as it seeks approval in European markets.Tesla has been campaigning to get approval for its Full Self-Driving software across Europe. A Reuters report detailed how the company encouraged vehicle owners and supporters to lobby national regulators to speed up the approval process.In September, a Norwegian Tesla owner asked the Norwegian Public Roads Administration whether the software name changes addressed regulators' concerns. In a request cited in documents Reuters obtained through freedom-of-information requests, the owner said:The European approval process remains ongoing, with individual countries conducting assessments and testing before wider authorisation.Eight EU countries already allow the system, while Slovakia was expected to become the ninth within days, according to the report. An EU-wide vote on the technology has been pushed from October to at least December. France is among the countries conducting additional testing.The name change is part of Tesla's broader effort to address regulatory concerns as it seeks wider approval. However, the rebranding alone does not mean the software has received EU-wide authorisation, and the timeline for broader approval remains uncertain.
Article Summary: Tesla has renamed its Full Self-Driving feature on several European websites. The electric vehicle maker now uses the name Tesla Assisted Driving in countries including Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, and Slovakia. The change comes as CEO Elon Musk seeks wider approval for the driver-assistance technology across the European Union.

Article Title: In 2014, Mark Zuckerberg called the movie 'hurtful', Sony is now trolling Meta CEO with an Instagram ad of its second part; promo says: Mark Zuckerberg will ...
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg

Sony's Instagram ad takes a dig at Mark Zuckerberg

Why Mark Zuckerberg called the first film hurtful

In 2014, Mark Zuckerberg said the film The Social Network, which portrayed Facebook's founding, was “kind of hurtful”. Now, Sony Pictures has taken a swipe at the Meta CEO through an Instagram ad promoting second part of the film – The Social Reckoning, which revisits the controversies surrounding the social media company. The ad features actor Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg and carries the message: “Mark Zuckerberg will LOVE The Social Reckoning*.” The punchline appears in the fine print: “*Instagram doesn’t fact-check most ads. Why should we?”The promotional video cuts between scenes of Jeremy Strong playing Mark Zuckerberg, including one in which the character wears headphones. The on-screen text initially suggests that the Meta CEO will enjoy the film, before the asterisk reveals the jab at Instagram's approach to fact-checking advertisements.The ad ends with Strong's Zuckerberg asking, “Did you know this was happening?” before the film's title appears.The film's Instagram page added another pointed line in its caption: “Let’s see how long it takes them to take this down.” According to the original report, the video had received more than 9,000 likes, 300 shares and 72 comments. Meta had not removed it at the time of the report, and the company did not respond to Fortune's request for comment.As stated above, Mark Zuckerberg had previously criticised The Social Network, the 2010 film written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher. In a public question-and-answer session in 2014, he said the filmmakers got some details right, including the design of Facebook's office, but “just kind of made up a bunch of stuff that I found kind of hurtful”. He specifically objected to the film's suggestion that he created Facebook to attract women.Aaron Sorkin has now returned to the subject with The Social Reckoning, which he wrote and directed. Sony describes it as a companion piece to the earlier film rather than a direct sequel.The new film focuses on Facebook's more recent controversies and is told largely through the perspective of Frances Haugen, played by Mikey Madison. Haugen, a former Facebook product manager, leaked tens of thousands of pages of internal documents to The Wall Street Journal and the US Securities and Exchange Commission in 2021. The documents helped expose concerns about the company's knowledge of problems linked to its platforms, including Instagram's effects on teenage girls' mental health.
Article Summary: Sony's Instagram ad takes a dig at Mark Zuckerberg. The ad features actor Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg and carries the message: “Mark Zuckerberg will LOVE The Social Reckoning*.” The punchline appears in the fine print: ‘*Instagram doesn’t fact-check most ads. Why should we?’
